fields.before:
Let states k count successes among n items, with truthful messages none, some and all. A uniform literal listener gives $L_0(k\mid u)=1/|\llbracket u\rrbracket|$ on compatible states. The modeled speaker uses
 $$S(u\mid k)\propto\exp\{\alpha[\log L_0(k\mid u)-c(u)]\},$$
 assigning zero weight to false messages. The pragmatic listener normalizes $P(k)S(\text{some}\mid k)$ over states compatible with the whole utterance. The supplied prior is binomial and the costs are authored. Plain some retains positive probability for all at every finite allowed setting, so the model does not turn the inference into an entailment. Adding in fact all restricts the state to n; adding but none leaves no compatible state and no posterior to normalize.
fields.after:
Let states k count successes among n items, with truthful messages none, some and all. A uniform literal listener gives $L_0(k\mid u)=1/|\llbracket u\rrbracket|$ on compatible states. Write $U(u,k)$ for $\log L_0(k\mid u)$ minus message cost $c(u)$. The modeled speaker uses
 $$S(u\mid k)\propto e^{\alpha U(u,k)},$$
 assigning zero weight to false messages. The pragmatic listener normalizes $P(k)S(\text{some}\mid k)$ over states compatible with the whole utterance. The supplied prior is binomial and the costs are authored. Plain some retains positive probability for all at every finite allowed setting, so the model does not turn the inference into an entailment. Adding in fact all restricts the state to n; adding but none leaves no compatible state and no posterior to normalize.

fields.before:
The exercise supplies four authored attributes and nonnegative importance weights. Its similarity to an all-feature prototype is
 $$T_w(x)=\frac{\sum_i w_i f_i(x)}{\sum_i w_i},\qquad \sum_iw_i>0.$$
 Increasing a weight emphasizes the corresponding attribute; multiplying every weight by the same positive factor preserves the ratio. With only flight emphasized, an illustrative bat can resemble the prototype more than a flightless bird, while the biological category labels remain fixed. This exposes the difference between the chosen representation’s similarity and membership. Setting every weight to zero leaves similarity undefined. Neither this feature table nor the weights are Rosch’s observed data, and the plotted values are not response times or collected judgments.

fields.before:
Let admissible cutoffs range over $[m-w,m+w]$. For positive w, h is supertrue when $h\ge m+w$, superfalse when $h<m-w$, and otherwise in a gap. Uniformly weighting these cutoffs gives the fraction
 $$F(h)=\min\!\left(1,\max\!\left(0,\frac{h-m+w}{2w}\right)\right).$$
 At the lower endpoint this fraction is zero, yet one admissible cutoff accepts and others reject: zero measure is not the same as no accepting definition. At $w=0$ there is one sharp rule. The separate logistic curve $1/[1+\exp(-(h-m)/s)]$ is an authored response model. Its continuity is an assumption of that model, not evidence that a hidden sharp boundary is impossible. The written sorites prerequisite explains why unrestricted tolerance creates a logical problem.
fields.after:
Let admissible cutoffs range over $[m-w,m+w]$. For positive w, h is supertrue when $h\ge m+w$, superfalse when $h<m-w$, and otherwise in a gap. Uniformly weighting these cutoffs gives the fraction
 $$z=\frac{h-m+w}{2w}.$$
 Set $F(h)=0$ for $z\le0$, $F(h)=z$ for $0<z<1$, and $F(h)=1$ for $z\ge1$. At the lower endpoint this fraction is zero, yet one admissible cutoff accepts and others reject: zero measure is not the same as no accepting definition. At $w=0$ there is one sharp rule. The separate logistic curve $1/[1+\exp(-(h-m)/s)]$ is an authored response model. Its continuity is an assumption of that model, not evidence that a hidden sharp boundary is impossible. The written sorites prerequisite explains why unrestricted tolerance creates a logical problem.
